*Version 2, updated October 2026. Data through MMWR week 39 (NNDSS export of October 10, 2026).*

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5, dpi = 120)
```

```{r load}
# Shared loader: reads both NNDSS exports, cleans them, builds `cyclo` and `latest_week`
source("scripts/00_load_and_clean.R")
```

```{r key-numbers, include=FALSE}
national <- cyclo %>% filter(area == "Total")
michigan <- cyclo %>% filter(area == "Michigan")

fmt <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")

season_2026 <- national %>% filter(year == current_year)
cum_now     <- season_2026 %>% filter(week == latest_week) %>% pull(cum_ytd)
peak        <- season_2026 %>% slice_max(weekly_additions, n = 1)

at_latest <- national %>% filter(week == latest_week) %>% select(year, cum_ytd)
baseline_avg <- at_latest %>% filter(year %in% baseline_years) %>% summarise(m = mean(cum_ytd)) %>% pull(m)
settled_2025 <- season_2026 %>% filter(week == latest_week) %>% pull(cum_prior_year_settled)

mi_cum     <- michigan %>% filter(year == current_year, week == latest_week) %>% pull(cum_ytd)
oh_cum     <- cyclo %>% filter(area == "Ohio", year == current_year, week == latest_week) %>% pull(cum_ytd)
lag_sum    <- sum(replace_na(season_2026$current_week, 0))
```

## What changed since the July version

The first version of this report was built from an NNDSS export published on
July 3, 2026, when only 25 weeks of 2026 data existed and the national
cumulative total stood at 992 cases. This update uses the October 10 export,
which runs through MMWR week `r latest_week`.

- **The season is far larger than the July snapshot suggested.** National
  cumulative cases reached **`r fmt(cum_now)`** through week `r latest_week`,
  which is **`r round(cum_now / baseline_avg, 1)`x** the 2022-2025 average at the
  same point (`r fmt(baseline_avg)`), with every year compared as first published.
- **The July conclusion held up, and then some.** The July report found Michigan
  far above its own history and suggested a broader pattern. Michigan now accounts
  for **`r round(100 * mi_cum / cum_now)`%** of national cumulative cases and Ohio
  for **`r round(100 * oh_cum / cum_now)`%**.
- **Provisional counts get revised a lot.** The July report said week 25 was likely
  an undercount. The data now show how much: 2025's week 25 cumulative total was
  first published as 272 and is now reported as 744.

## Background

Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by the microscopic parasite
*Cyclospora cayetanensis*. A few facts shape how this analysis is framed:

- **Transmission is foodborne or waterborne only.** People are infected by eating
  food or drinking water contaminated with feces that contain the parasite. Freshly
  shed oocysts are not immediately infectious (it takes 1-2 weeks in the
  environment), so direct person-to-person spread does not occur. Case curves
  therefore tend to reflect exposure to shared contaminated food, clustered in time,
  rather than an exponential transmission chain.
- **Incubation** is 2-14 days (average about 1 week) from exposure to symptoms.
- **Seasonality:** U.S. cases cluster May to August every year. That alone is not
  evidence of an unusual outbreak, which is why this report builds a seasonal
  baseline from prior years.

## Data

Data come from the **National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS)**
weekly tables on
[data.cdc.gov](https://data.cdc.gov/NNDSS/NNDSS-Weekly-Data/x9gk-5huc).
Two exports are used:

| File | Used for |
|---|---|
| `NNDSS_Weekly_Data_2022-2026_20260703.csv` | Baseline years 2022-2025 |
| `NNDSS_Weekly_Data_2026_20261010.csv` | 2026, weeks 1-`r latest_week` |

The October export contains only 2026. That is fine because NNDSS rows are
snapshots of what was published in each week and are not rewritten later. The check
below confirms it by comparing the 2026 rows (weeks 1-25) in the two exports.

```{r july-check}
july_2026 <- read_nndss(baseline_file) %>%
  filter(year == current_year, label == "Cyclosporiasis", week <= 52)

check <- july_2026 %>%
  inner_join(current %>% filter(label == "Cyclosporiasis"),
             by = c("area", "week"), suffix = c("_jul", "_oct")) %>%
  summarise(
    rows_compared = n(),
    rows_changed  = sum(coalesce(current_week_jul, -1) != coalesce(current_week_oct, -1) |
                        coalesce(cum_ytd_jul, -1)      != coalesce(cum_ytd_oct, -1))
  )
check
```

### Data-cleaning issues

These affect every number in the report, and are worth knowing for any multi-year
government export.

1. **Inconsistent capitalization across years.** 2022-2024 use ALL CAPS
   (`"MICHIGAN"`), 2025-2026 use Title Case (`"Michigan"`). An exact-match filter
   would silently drop years. Fixed with `str_to_title()`.
2. **Thousands separators stored as text.** Counts over 999 appear as `"1,171"`, and
   `as.numeric("1,171")` silently returns `NA`. Fixed by stripping commas.
3. **The `-` flag does not reliably mean zero.** It appears on blank cells (where it
   does mean zero) and on populated cells (where it is only an annotation). The rule
   used here: trust a populated value, and read the flag only for blank cells.
4. **Aggregate labels do not unify with case normalization.** `"US RESIDENTS"`
   becomes `"Us Residents"`, not `"U.S. Residents"`. This report uses only the
   `"Total"` row and the 50 states plus DC, which do unify.

The cleaning function (from `scripts/00_load_and_clean.R`):

```{r clean-function-excerpt, eval=FALSE}
clean_flagged_col <- function(value_col, flag_col) {
  numeric_val <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(str_remove_all(as.character(value_col), ",")))
  case_when(
    !is.na(numeric_val)             ~ numeric_val,   # a real value was reported: always trust it
    flag_col == "-"                 ~ 0,              # blank + "-" flag = zero
    flag_col %in% c("N", "NC", "U") ~ NA_real_,       # not reportable / not calculated / unavailable
    TRUE ~ NA_real_
  )
}
```

## How NNDSS counts get revised

Because each weekly row is frozen at publication, early-season counts look much
smaller than they eventually become. The only place revisions are visible is the
"previous year" cumulative column in the next year's rows. Comparing 2025 as first
published (2025 rows) with 2025 as settled (2026 rows) shows the size of the effect.

```{r vintage}
vintage <- national %>%
  filter(year == 2025, week <= latest_week) %>%
  select(week, first_published = cum_ytd) %>%
  inner_join(season_2026 %>% select(week, settled = cum_prior_year_settled), by = "week") %>%
  mutate(ratio = settled / first_published)

vintage %>%
  filter(week %in% c(25, 30, 35, latest_week)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("MMWR week", "First published", "Settled", "Settled / first published"),
               format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r vintage-plot}
vintage_long <- vintage %>%
  pivot_longer(c(first_published, settled), names_to = "version", values_to = "cum") %>%
  mutate(version = recode(version,
                          first_published = "As first published in 2025",
                          settled = "As settled (reported in 2026)"))

ggplot(vintage_long, aes(week, cum, color = version)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("As first published in 2025" = "grey55",
                                "As settled (reported in 2026)" = "grey15")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "2025 cumulative cases: first published vs. settled",
       subtitle = "Early-season counts are revised upward the most",
       x = "MMWR week", y = "Cumulative cases", color = NULL,
       caption = paste0("Source: NNDSS Weekly Data, data.cdc.gov (export ", export_date, ")")) +
  theme_epi() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Two consequences follow. First, all baseline comparisons in this report use every
year **as first published**, so the comparison is like for like. Second, the 2026
numbers are provisional in the same way, and will be revised upward as well. The
`r round(cum_now / baseline_avg, 1)`x figure is a same-vintage comparison; against 2025 as
settled (`r fmt(settled_2025)`), 2026 is `r sprintf("%.1f", cum_now / settled_2025)`x, but that
mixes a provisional count with a settled one.

## The 2026 season nationally

The weekly measure used here is **reports added to the cumulative total each
week** (the week-over-week change in the cumulative column). It is a reporting
curve, not an epidemic curve by onset date, so it includes late reports for earlier
weeks. The reason it is used instead of the `Current week` column is shown in the
next section.

```{r national-weekly}
band <- national %>%
  filter(year %in% baseline_years, week <= latest_week) %>%
  group_by(week) %>%
  summarise(lo = min_na(weekly_additions), hi = max_na(weekly_additions), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(season_2026 %>% select(week, weekly_additions), by = "week")

ggplot(band, aes(x = week)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = weekly_additions), color = accent_color, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Reports added to the national total each week, 2026 vs. 2022-2025",
       subtitle = "Grey band = min-max range across 2022-2025. Red line = 2026.",
       x = "MMWR week", y = "Reports added that week",
       caption = paste0("Source: NNDSS Weekly Data, data.cdc.gov (export ", export_date, "). Provisional data.")) +
  theme_epi()
```

Reports added peaked in MMWR week **`r peak$week`** at **`r fmt(peak$weekly_additions)`**
in a single week, then fell sharply by week 36. The same story in cumulative form:

```{r national-cumulative}
year_colors <- c("2022" = "grey75", "2023" = "grey60", "2024" = "grey45",
                 "2025" = "grey25", "2026" = accent_color)

national %>%
  filter(week <= latest_week) %>%
  mutate(year_lab = factor(year)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(week, cum_ytd, color = year_lab, linewidth = year_lab)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_manual(values = year_colors) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c("2022" = 0.6, "2023" = 0.6, "2024" = 0.6, "2025" = 0.6, "2026" = 1.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative cases by MMWR week, 2022-2026",
       subtitle = "Every year shown as first published, so the years are directly comparable",
       x = "MMWR week", y = "Cumulative cases (year to date)", color = NULL,
       caption = paste0("Source: NNDSS Weekly Data, data.cdc.gov (export ", export_date, ")")) +
  guides(linewidth = "none") +
  theme_epi() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r season-table}
season_2026 %>%
  filter(week %in% c(25, 28, 30, 33, 36, latest_week)) %>%
  select(week, current_week, weekly_additions, cum_ytd) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("MMWR week", "'Current week' column", "Reports added", "Cumulative"),
               format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

## Why "Current week" undercounts

The `Current week` column is frozen at the moment of publication, while the
cumulative total absorbs reports that arrive late. Through week `r latest_week`, the
`Current week` values sum to **`r fmt(lag_sum)`**, only
**`r round(100 * lag_sum / cum_now)`%** of the **`r fmt(cum_now)`** cumulative total.
The gap grew every week, which is why the report uses cumulative differences for
weekly trends.

```{r reporting-lag}
lag_long <- season_2026 %>%
  arrange(week) %>%
  mutate(running_sum_current_week = cumsum(replace_na(current_week, 0))) %>%
  select(week, running_sum_current_week, cum_ytd) %>%
  pivot_longer(-week, names_to = "series", values_to = "cases") %>%
  mutate(series = recode(series,
                         running_sum_current_week = "Running sum of 'Current week'",
                         cum_ytd = "Reported cumulative total"))

ggplot(lag_long, aes(week, cases, color = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Running sum of 'Current week'" = "grey55",
                                "Reported cumulative total" = accent_color)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Why 'Current week' undercounts",
       subtitle = "The gap is reports that arrived late and were folded into the cumulative total only",
       x = "MMWR week", y = "Cases", color = NULL,
       caption = paste0("Source: NNDSS Weekly Data, data.cdc.gov (export ", export_date, ")")) +
  theme_epi() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Michigan

In the July report, Michigan's week-25 count was 0, 0, 1 and 0 in 2022-2025
against 46 in 2026. Three months later:

```{r michigan-table}
michigan %>%
  filter(week == latest_week) %>%
  select(year, cum_ytd) %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(year = as.character(year)) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Year", paste0("Cumulative cases through week ", latest_week, " (as first published)")),
               format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r michigan-weekly}
mi_2026 <- michigan %>% filter(year == current_year) %>% select(week, current_week, weekly_additions, cum_ytd)

mi_band <- michigan %>%
  filter(year %in% baseline_years, week <= latest_week) %>%
  group_by(week) %>%
  summarise(lo = min_na(weekly_additions), hi = max_na(weekly_additions), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(mi_2026 %>% select(week, weekly_additions), by = "week")

ggplot(mi_band, aes(x = week)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = weekly_additions), color = accent_color, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Michigan: reports added each week, 2026 vs. 2022-2025",
       subtitle = "Grey band = min-max range across 2022-2025. Red line = 2026.",
       x = "MMWR week", y = "Reports added that week",
       caption = paste0("Source: NNDSS Weekly Data, data.cdc.gov (export ", export_date, "). Provisional data.")) +
  theme_epi()
```

Michigan's cumulative total (`r fmt(mi_cum)`) is
`r round(100 * mi_cum / cum_now)`% of the national total, and its prior-year range
at this point in the season was only
`r fmt(min(michigan$cum_ytd[michigan$year %in% baseline_years & michigan$week == latest_week]))`-`r fmt(max(michigan$cum_ytd[michigan$year %in% baseline_years & michigan$week == latest_week]))`
cases.

**One thing to watch:** Michigan's reports added fell to between
`r fmt(min(mi_2026$weekly_additions[mi_2026$week %in% (latest_week - 3):(latest_week - 1)]))` and
`r fmt(max(mi_2026$weekly_additions[mi_2026$week %in% (latest_week - 3):(latest_week - 1)]))` per week in
weeks `r latest_week - 3`-`r latest_week - 1`, then rose again in week `r latest_week`
(`r fmt(mi_2026$weekly_additions[mi_2026$week == latest_week])`). The `Current week`
column also jumps (`r fmt(mi_2026$current_week[mi_2026$week == latest_week - 1])` to
`r fmt(mi_2026$current_week[mi_2026$week == latest_week])`). This file cannot say
whether that is a late batch of reports or a new increase, so it needs rechecking
once weeks 40 and later are published.

## State comparison

Each state is compared with itself: its 2026 cumulative count against its own
2022-2025 mean at the same MMWR week, all as first published.

```{r state-ranking}
state_data <- cyclo %>% filter(area %in% us_states)

now_vals <- state_data %>% filter(year == current_year, week == latest_week) %>%
  select(area, cases_2026 = cum_ytd)
baseline_vals <- state_data %>% filter(year %in% baseline_years, week == latest_week) %>%
  group_by(area) %>% summarise(baseline_avg = mean(cum_ytd, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

state_ranking <- now_vals %>%
  full_join(baseline_vals, by = "area") %>%
  mutate(
    cases_2026   = replace_na(cases_2026, 0),
    baseline_avg = replace_na(baseline_avg, 0),
    share_of_national = cases_2026 / cum_now,
    ratio_label = case_when(
      baseline_avg == 0 & cases_2026 == 0 ~ "no change (both 0)",
      baseline_avg == 0 & cases_2026 > 0  ~ "new (baseline was 0)",
      TRUE ~ paste0(round(cases_2026 / baseline_avg, 1), "x")
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cases_2026))

state_ranking %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  select(area, baseline_avg, cases_2026, share_of_national, ratio_label) %>%
  mutate(share_of_national = scales::percent(share_of_national, accuracy = 0.1)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1,
               col.names = c("State", "2022-25 mean", paste0("2026 through wk ", latest_week), "Share of national", "vs. baseline"),
               format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

top5_share <- sum(head(state_ranking$cases_2026, 5)) / cum_now
n_states_up <- sum(state_ranking$cases_2026 > state_ranking$baseline_avg & state_ranking$cases_2026 > 0)
n_reporting <- sum(!is.na(now_vals$cases_2026))
```

The top five states account for **`r round(100 * top5_share)`%** of the national
cumulative total, and `r n_states_up` of the `r n_reporting` states and DC that
report cyclosporiasis to NNDSS are above their own 2022-2025 level. Michigan and Ohio dominate, but the rise is not limited to them.

```{r state-multiples, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
top_states <- state_ranking %>% slice_max(cases_2026, n = 9) %>% pull(area)
top_weekly <- state_data %>% filter(area %in% top_states, week <= latest_week)

state_band <- top_weekly %>%
  filter(year %in% baseline_years) %>%
  group_by(area, week) %>%
  summarise(lo = min_na(weekly_additions), hi = max_na(weekly_additions), .groups = "drop")

state_band %>%
  left_join(top_weekly %>% filter(year == current_year) %>% select(area, week, weekly_additions),
            by = c("area", "week")) %>%
  mutate(area = factor(area, levels = top_states)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = weekly_additions), color = accent_color, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ area, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "2026 vs. 2022-2025 range: top 9 states by cumulative cases",
       subtitle = "Reports added each week. Grey band = min-max across 2022-2025. Red = 2026. Y-axis scales differ by state.",
       x = "MMWR week", y = "Reports added that week",
       caption = paste0("Source: NNDSS Weekly Data, data.cdc.gov (export ", export_date, "). Provisional data.")) +
  theme_epi(base_size = 11) + theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

State-level weekly series are lumpy because states send reports in batches. Illinois,
for example, added 386 reports in week 35 and none in weeks 36-39, and North Carolina
alternates between large weeks and near-zero weeks. Read single weeks at the state
level with caution; the cumulative totals are more reliable.

## What this analysis can and cannot say

- **It describes reporting, not exposure.** NNDSS weekly tables carry no onset
  dates and no food-source information. Public reporting from late July linked a
  subcluster of the outbreak to shredded iceberg lettuce, while a broader
  investigation into other clusters had not identified a product (see Sources).
  Nothing in this dataset can confirm or refine that.
- **All counts are provisional and will rise.** 2025's week-25 total was revised
  upward by a factor of about 2.7. Expect the same for 2026, with early weeks
  revised the most.
- **NNDSS and CDC outbreak-page counts are different measures** and will not match.
  CDC's outbreak reporting uses its own case definitions and counting windows.
- **Three states have no NNDSS values for cyclosporiasis:** Idaho, Mississippi and
  Pennsylvania carry the "not reportable" flag. Kentucky also has no 2022 values, so
  its baseline uses three years. New York City reports separately from New York
  State and is excluded from the state ranking.
- **One baseline anomaly:** Colorado's 2024 cumulative total jumped by
  `r fmt(cyclo %>% filter(area == "Colorado", year == 2024, week == 39) %>% pull(weekly_additions))`
  in week 39 and was reversed in week 49. As first published, it inflates the national
  2024 baseline at week 39 by 144 cases (a shift of about 36 cases in the four-year
  average), which does not change any conclusion here.
- **The last published week is the least reliable.** The week-`r latest_week` uptick
  nationally and in Michigan should be rechecked once later weeks are available.

## Next steps

- Re-pull NNDSS when weeks 40 and later are published, and save it as a new dated file.
- Compare this snapshot with the next to see how much 2026 gets revised.
- Map state-level cumulative counts with `tigris` and `sf`.
- If county-level data become public for Michigan or Ohio, add them as a separate,
  clearly labeled dataset.
